clue.text: Watchword "the king, in bloody surroundings" — for Russian writer

parts.note: a watchword is a guiding saying or motto, a maxim

indicators.note: the king is placed in the middle of a word for bloody
the bloody word forms the surroundings that close round the king

parts.note: bloody means gory
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A motto about a monarch amid gore is offered up on behalf of a Russian author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watchword' looks like the definition, but it supplies a saying; the Russian writer is the definition at the end, with 'for' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxim Gorky was the pen name of Alexei Peshkov, the Soviet-era novelist and playwright.

clue.text: Was Miss Johnson's petrified?

parts.note: Pamela Hansford Johnson wrote the 1947 novel An ... of Stone, so her thoroughfare was turned to stone

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a lady called Johnson was frozen with fright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'petrified' looks like terrified, but it means turned to stone: Pamela Hansford Johnson's novel is An Avenue of Stone.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Johnson's novel names a tree-lined road made of stone, a petrified thoroughfare.

clue.text: A splendid one of Lloyd C. Douglas in translation

definitions.text: A splendid one of Lloyd C. Douglas in translation

parts.words: A splendid one of Lloyd C. Douglas in translation
parts.note: Lloyd C. Douglas wrote Magnificent Obsession; the French phrase for an obsession is wanted

explanation.surface: A fine example of an American novelist's work is rendered in another language.
explanation.walkthrough: Lloyd C. Douglas's novel is Magnificent Obsession; 'in translation' asks for the French term for an obsession.
explanation.definitionFit: The French borrowing names a fixed, obsessive notion, which translates the obsession in Douglas's title.

clue.text: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall

definitions.text: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall

parts.words: Post with certain perks at Wragby Hall
parts.note: Wragby Hall is the Chatterley estate in Lawrence's Lady Chatterley's Lover, where Mellors holds this job and enjoys Lady Chatterley

explanation.surface: A job advertisement mentions fringe benefits at a country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Mellors, the estate's game warden in Lady Chatterley's Lover, has an affair with his employer's wife: the 'certain perks'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mellors' job at Wragby is looking after the game birds on the estate.

clue.text: For pillage, the answer is in an instrument of torture

indicators.note: the abbreviation sits inside the torture device

parts.note: the rack is a medieval device for stretching a victim
ANS is the usual abbreviation of answer

explanation.surface: A grim aside: looting finds its explanation in a torturer's tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For pillage' looks like a noun phrase, but the definition is the verb sense: to plunder.
explanation.definitionFit: To ransack is to plunder or loot a place thoroughly.

clue.text: "A whale ship was my — college and my Harvard" (Herman Melville)

definitions.text: "A whale ship was my — college and my Harvard" (Herman Melville)

parts.words: "A whale ship was my — college and my Harvard" (Herman Melville)
parts.note: Ishmael in Moby-Dick names the other great American university alongside Harvard

explanation.surface: A line from Moby-Dick with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Moby-Dick, chapter 24; the missing word is the Connecticut university paired with Harvard.
explanation.definitionFit: The New Haven university is the rival of Harvard named in Melville's line.

clue.text: Goddess conceals a prohibition of Latin dance

indicators.note: the goddess's name hides the other letters within it

parts.note: Hera is the Greek queen of the gods
a ban is a prohibition

explanation.surface: A deity hides an embargo on a South American dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The goddess is Greek, the queen of Olympus; the inserted letters go in after her first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The habanera is a slow Cuban dance in duple time, as in Carmen.

clue.text: Phrygians upset in casino loss

indicators.note: upset signals the letters of casino loss are overturned and rearranged

explanation.surface: Ancient Phrygians are dismayed by a gambling defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges CASINO LOSS. Colossae was a city in Phrygia, and Paul's epistle is addressed to its people.
explanation.definitionFit: The Colossians were inhabitants of Colossae, a town in the ancient region of Phrygia in Asia Minor.

clue.text: A gentleman and a gamester, according to his page, and provided with weapons in Spain

definitions.text: A gentleman and a gamester, according to his page
definitions.meaning: in Love's Labour's Lost the page Moth tells Don Adriano de ... he is a gentleman and a gamester

explanation.surface: A servant's account of his master, a gentleman gambler who goes armed in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: Don Armado is the boastful Spaniard of Love's Labour's Lost; his name is also Spanish for armed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Shakespearean Spaniard's name doubles as the Spanish past participle meaning equipped with arms.

clue.text: Humorist father of the French student chap

parts.note: pere is French for father
L for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: A comic writer's French-speaking dad has a son at college.
explanation.definitionFit: S. J. Perelman was an American comic writer for The New Yorker and the Marx Brothers.

clue.text: Prototypical drunken butler

parts.note: in The Tempest, the butler who staggers about tipsy is an early model of the inebriate servant

explanation.surface: The original sozzled manservant of fiction.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Tempest gives the tipsy butler who teams up with Trinculo and Caliban.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephano is the wine-sodden steward in The Tempest, a model for later stage drunks.

clue.text: Vile misinterpretation of Italian novelist

indicators.note: a misreading of the word vile suggests its letters taken in the wrong order

explanation.surface: A nasty misreading of an Italian writer's work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misinterpretation of' rearranges VILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Primo Levi and Carlo Levi were both Italian writers of fiction and memoir.

clue.text: Sarah Woodruff apparently belonged to a French one

definitions.text: Sarah Woodruff apparently belonged to a French one

parts.words: Sarah Woodruff apparently belonged to a French one
parts.note: John Fowles's heroine Sarah Woodruff is known as The French ... Woman

explanation.surface: A Victorian woman is said to have been the property of a Frenchman.
explanation.walkthrough: Sarah Woodruff is the heroine of Fowles's The French Lieutenant's Woman; 'apparently' because the story of the officer is gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Fowles's novel names the French naval officer whose woman she is supposed to be.

clue.text: Stephen Spender arranged several such meetings

definitions.text: Stephen Spender arranged several such meetings

parts.words: Stephen Spender arranged several such meetings
parts.note: Spender co-founded and co-edited a famous Cold War literary monthly whose title means a chance meeting, so he put together many issues

explanation.surface: A poet organised a number of get-togethers.
explanation.walkthrough: Spender co-edited the literary magazine of that name from 1953; each issue he put together is one of the 'meetings'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chance meetings share their name with the magazine Spender edited.

clue.text: Across's chap surplus to requirements

parts.note: the writer at one across wrote The Life of a ...; the chap is that redundant figure

explanation.surface: A fellow from the other direction is no longer needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across' points to 1 across, the Russian writer, whose novel is The Life of a Useless Man.
explanation.definitionFit: A man surplus to requirements is good for nothing, the subject of the Russian novel's title.

clue.text: Muse among palms

definitions.meaning: one of the nine Muses, the one of music and lyric poetry
also the name of a genus of tropical palm trees, including the acai

explanation.surface: An inspiring goddess stands amid palm trees.
explanation.definitionFit: Euterpe is the Greek Muse of music, and the name was borrowed for a genus of South American palms.

clue.text: Murderous Jack, in first tentative sortie, discovers tourists

indicators.note: the killer's name goes in between two letters
first picks the opening letters of tentative and sortie

parts.note: Jack the Ripper, the Victorian London murderer

explanation.surface: A killer's first hesitant outing turns up some sightseers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes T and S from tentative sortie, and 'in' puts RIPPER between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Trippers are day visitors on an excursion, sightseers.

clue.text: Baker's pause

definitions.meaning: in music, a sign that a note is held longer than written

explanation.surface: A baker takes a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baker' is the novelist Nicholson Baker, not a bread maker; his novel's hero can stop time.
explanation.definitionFit: A fermata is the musical hold sign, and Baker's novel takes its name from it.

clue.text: "My lady's a Catalan, we are politicians, —'s a Peg-a- Ramsey" (Twelfth Night)

definitions.text: "My lady's a Catalan, we are politicians, —'s a Peg-a- Ramsey" (Twelfth Night)

parts.words: "My lady's a Catalan, we are politicians, —'s a Peg-a- Ramsey" (Twelfth Night)
parts.note: Sir Toby Belch mocks Olivia's puritanical steward in Act 2, Scene 3

explanation.surface: A line from Twelfth Night with a name left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Toby says this when the steward threatens to report the revellers; 'Peg-a-Ramsey' is a scornful term from a ballad.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivia's pompous steward is the man Sir Toby ridicules in the scene.

clue.text: Marvellous quality of Southern Christian?

parts.note: Terry Southern wrote The Magic Christian, so the adjective describes that book's title

explanation.surface: Asking what makes a believer from the South so wonderful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern' is the novelist Terry Southern, author of The Magic Christian, not a region.
explanation.definitionFit: Marvellous and enchanting both describe something with the power of sorcery.

clue.text: Fitting, hopefully, like the product of le Carré' Harry Pendel

definitions.meaning: perfectly suited, as if made for the purpose

definitions.text: like the product of le Carré' Harry Pendel
definitions.meaning: Harry Pendel is the suit-maker in le Carre's The Tailor of Panama, so his goods are bespoke

explanation.surface: Hoping that something suits, like the work of a fictional spy's outfitter.
explanation.walkthrough: Pendel is the Savile Row-style outfitter in The Tailor of Panama; 'hopefully' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ideally suited is described as made to measure, like a bespoke suit.

clue.text: Grassy areas where Elsa wandered

indicators.note: wandered signals the letters of Elsa roam into a new order

explanation.surface: A woman named Elsa strolled across meadows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandered' rearranges ELSA.
explanation.definitionFit: Leas are meadows or pasture land, a poetic word for fields.

clue.text: Romance of a loud blonde ended by Greene

parts.note: F stands for forte, loud in music
fair means light-haired

explanation.surface: A love story about a noisy fair-haired woman, concluded by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ended by Greene' recalls Greene's The End of the Affair, adding to the surface rather than the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A romance is a love affair, a liaison.

clue.text: New Thai plan from multi-genre artistic director

indicators.note: new indicates the letters of Thai plan are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A fresh plan from Thailand comes from a versatile arts director.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges THAI PLAN.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs to a theatre and arts director working across several genres.

clue.text: An obstruction for an architect

parts.note: a dam is a barrier blocking water

explanation.surface: A barrier stands in the way of a building designer.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Adam was an eighteenth-century Scottish designer of buildings and interiors.

clue.text: Finished, like sportsman in part portrayed by Cotton

definitions.text: like sportsman in part portrayed by Cotton
definitions.meaning: Charles Cotton wrote the second part of Walton's The ... Angler

explanation.surface: A completed portrait of an athlete, partly drawn by a man named Cotton.
explanation.walkthrough: Izaak Walton's The Compleat Angler gained a second part on fly fishing by Charles Cotton.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic spelling means complete or accomplished, as in Walton's title.

clue.text: Chilean writer, unfortunately unread

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests the letters of unread have gone awry

explanation.surface: A South American author sadly goes unread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges UNREAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Neruda was the Nobel-winning Chilean poet.

clue.text: Mr Brooks before the judge as Sir Oran Haut-Ton?

parts.note: Mel Brooks, the American comedian and film-maker
appearing in court means standing before a judge

explanation.surface: A comedian appears in court dressed as an aristocratic orangutan.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Oran Haut-Ton is the orangutan made a baronet in Peacock's novel Melincourt; the definition is by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Peacock's satirical novel features the ape who becomes an MP, so the character stands for the book.
